analysis.one_liner: Raises penalties for false and deceptive advertising of COVID-related products during the pandemic emergency.
analysis.headline: The bipartisan bill to raise fines and prison terms for false COVID-19 advertising was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in June 2020 and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 emergency, scammers sold fake cures, bogus test kits, and other pandemic-related products through false advertising. This bill would have increased the criminal penalties for false advertising and the civil fines the Federal Trade Commission can impose for unfair or deceptive practices tied to COVID-19, and it would have made deceptive COVID-19-related commercial practices explicitly illegal for the duration of the emergency. The penalties would have run up to a $50,000 fine and one year in prison for a first offense, and a $250,000 fine and one to five years in prison for repeat offenses.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers, especially people frightened by the pandemic and looking for test kits, protective equipment, treatments, or cures. Anyone targeted by ads falsely claiming a product prevents, treats, or cures COVID-19 would gain from stronger deterrents against the sellers of those products, since the risk of bigger fines and criminal prosecution is meant to keep such products off the market.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the criminal penalty for false advertising during the COVID-19 emergency from up to six months in prison and a $5,000 fine for a first offense to up to one year in prison and a $50,000 fine, and from up to one year and $10,000 to one to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine for repeat offenses.

Raises the civil penalty the Federal Trade Commission can seek for unfair or deceptive acts, and for unfair methods of competition, during the emergency from $10,000 to $50,000 for a first offense and $250,000 for subsequent offenses.

Makes it explicitly unlawful during the emergency to engage in any unfair or deceptive act or practice that relates to the COVID-19 pandemic, and gives the FTC the same enforcement powers it has under the FTC Act to pursue violations.

analysis.who_pays: Companies and individuals that advertise falsely or deceptively about COVID-19-related products and services bear the cost, in the form of larger civil fines, criminal fines, and prison terms. Businesses that advertise honestly would bear no new cost; the bill's penalties apply only to false or deceptive practices.

drawbacks.text: The penalty increases are temporary: they apply only during the declared COVID-19 public health emergency and lapse when it ends, so the underlying weak penalty levels for false advertising would remain afterward.

The bill raises penalties but provides no direct restitution to consumers who already lost money to COVID-19 scams; enforcement would run entirely through the FTC and criminal prosecutors rather than putting money back in victims' pockets.

Supporters of stronger deterrence would acknowledge that larger fines only matter if regulators bring cases; the bill adds no new enforcement staff or mandates for the FTC, so its practical effect depends entirely on how aggressively the agency uses its existing authority.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but modest: it would have made advertising fraud tied to a once-in-a-century health emergency meaningfully more expensive to commit, at essentially no cost to honest businesses. The cost side is small by design, but so is the reach: the deterrent depends on the FTC actually prosecuting, victims get no restitution, and everything expires with the emergency.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2020 and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never took it up, and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Gardner introduced the CEASE Act on June 2, 2020, joined by Democratic Senator Kyrsten Sinema and Republican Senator Shelley Moore Capito.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day it was introduced.
No further action was ever recorded: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action, and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sellers who used false or deceptive COVID-19 advertising kept operating under the old, low penalty levels of up to a $10,000 civil fine and six months in prison for a first offense. Consumers remained exposed to pandemic-related advertising fraud without the enhanced deterrents this bill would have created.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start — a Republican sponsor with one Democratic and one Republican cosponsor — and no one spoke or voted against it; it simply never advanced out of committee.

industries.industry: Deceptive marketers and sellers of COVID-19-related products (fake cures, test kits, protective gear)
industries.note: The bill raises the civil fines and criminal penalties these sellers face by five- to twenty-five-fold during the emergency, directly targeting advertising that preys on people seeking pandemic protection and treatment. Their gain from the bill's failure is the public's continued exposure to fraud.

The bill only penalizes false or deceptive COVID-19-related advertising, so truthful businesses face no new liability. To the extent it clears scam competitors out of the market during a crisis, honest sellers benefit alongside consumers.

The bill gives the FTC a higher civil penalty ceiling ($50,000 first offense, $250,000 repeat) and an explicit COVID-19 deception prohibition to enforce during the emergency, strengthening its consumer-protection toolkit.
